entry.title: Kawicki v Trustees of the Marist Brothers t/as Marist Brothers Sydney Province [2026] NSWCA 220
entry.content:
The appellant, a former student, sued the Trustees of the Marist Brothers for damages arising from sexual abuse by Brother Florentine; the primary judge awarded $186,000 but declined damages for diminished earning capacity. The Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal against the refusal of past economic loss, with Adamson JA dissenting. The appeal concerned only economic loss; liability for the sexual abuse and the $186,000 award were not in issue.

Key holding: A claimant alleging past economic loss from historical abuse bears the onus of proving that the abuse caused a diminution in earning capacity productive of actual financial loss; a tribunal may reject the claim by not being satisfied, without making a positive finding of no diminution.

A failure to be satisfied that there was a diminution in earning capacity is different from a finding that there was no diminution in earning capacity. The onus to establish a diminution in earning capacity rested on Mr Kawicki.

entry.title: Lamont v The Royal Women's Hospital (No 4) [2026] VSC 687
entry.content:
In the principal negligence proceeding, after judgment was reserved, the plaintiff applied to defer delivery of judgment pending a possible application to reopen based on four documents. The defendants sought costs against the plaintiff’s solicitors, Shine Lawyers. The Supreme Court of Victoria found the deferral application was an abuse of process and ordered Shine Lawyers to pay both defendants’ costs on an indemnity basis.

Key holding: A court may make a personal indemnity costs order against a solicitor where the solicitor advances an application that is an abuse of process and lacking in merit, in breach of the solicitor’s duty to the Court.

In circumstances in which I have concluded that the deferral application was both an abuse of process and lacking in merit, and that Shine Lawyers acted in a way that was in breach of its duty to the Court, I am satisfied that an order for indemnity costs should be made.

entry.title: Solomon v Bendigo & Adelaide Bank Limited [2026] NSWSC 1301
entry.content:
This was a discovery ruling in Mrs Solomon’s Commercial List claim against Bendigo & Adelaide Bank Limited for $6.2 million lost in a sophisticated term deposit scam. The Court refused several disputed discovery categories in their current form and held that the plaintiff must further amend her pleading to identify, with specificity, the institutional precautions the Bank should have taken. The Bank was ordered to answer interrogatories and to reconsider its denial of knowledge about term deposit scams.

Key holding: In a negligence claim, including institutional negligence, a plaintiff must specifically identify the precautions that should have been taken and show why reasonable care required them, assessed prospectively rather than by hindsight.

An essential requirement for liability in negligence is that the plaintiff must identify with specificity the allegedly negligent acts or omissions of the defendant, and demonstrate that those acts or omissions involved a failure to take reasonable care.

entry.title: Chalker v Baldwin [No 3] [2026] VSC 670
entry.content:
In Chalker v Baldwin [No 3] [2026] VSC 670, a self-represented plaintiff in a medical treatment and assault proceeding sought further discovery from Barwon Health, leave to issue subpoenas, and an extension of time to join a third defendant. Tsalamandris J largely confined discovery to documents relevant to the pleaded issues, rejected broad or peripheral categories, refused the Victoria Police subpoena, and refused the joinder extension.

Key holding: Further discovery is confined to documents relevant to the issues as pleaded, and requests that are peripheral or disproportionate to the central issues will not be ordered.

Accordingly, demands for discovery of documents which are peripheral to the central issues cannot be entertained. The Court is obliged to focus on the central issues as best it can be determined at this point in the litigation.

entry.title: Caller v State of NSW [2026] NSWCA 212
entry.content:
The appellant, a former NSW police officer, suffered PTSD from cumulative exposure to traumatic incidents during service. The primary judge found the State breached its duty by failing to implement its own record-keeping system to monitor cumulative trauma exposure, but held the breach did not cause the PTSD. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, upholding the no-causation finding and rejecting challenges to other alleged breaches.

Key holding: In a negligence claim, the plaintiff must prove not only breach of duty but also that the breach caused the loss claimed.

In order to succeed on the negligence claim brought by the appellant, it was necessary for him to establish that there was a breach of duty owed to him which caused the loss (in this case, his developing PTSD).

entry.title: Costantino v Hillier (No 2) [2026] NSWSC 1260
entry.content:
This is a costs decision following the Court’s earlier determination of limitations issues in a professional negligence claim. The plaintiff failed to obtain an extension of the long-stop limitation period for claims concerning the first four surgeries, while the defendant’s separate question also affected claims concerning the fifth and sixth surgeries. The Court ordered the costs of the plaintiff’s notice of motion and the separate question to be costs in the cause, rather than acceding to the defendant’s proposed 75% costs order.

Key holding: Where parties achieve mixed success on overlapping interlocutory limitation applications, the Court may exercise its costs discretion by ordering costs in the cause rather than apportioning costs issue-by-issue.

In my view, the parties have each achieved some success and some failure in their competing applications which were heard before me on 18 and 19 August 2026. While there is some significant overlap between them, I nevertheless consider the most appropriate way to approach the costs of those applications is to order that they be costs in the cause.

entry.title: Palmer v State of Queensland [2026] QSC 30
entry.content:
The plaintiff sued the State of Queensland for psychiatric injury allegedly caused by a rape on Palm Island in about 1959 or 1960, when she was a child. The State applied for summary judgment or strike-out, denying any duty of care and alleging no causal link. The Supreme Court entered judgment for the State and ordered the plaintiff to pay costs.

Key holding: If the material does not suggest a party could plead a legally recognised cause of action, leave to replead should be refused and judgment for the defendant may follow.

Where there is nothing in the material before the court to suggest that a party could plead a cause of action known to law, leave to replead would be refused. Indeed, a logical consequence may be to give judgment for the defendant.

entry.title: SC (name suppressed) v Integroe Partners Pty Ltd t/as Integroe Partners [2026] NSWDC 367
entry.content:
The Plaintiff, the mother of a child (PS) treated at a Sydney Catholic Schools school, sued Integroe Partners Pty Ltd in negligence over investigations it conducted for SCS into the school’s use of a sensory room and lockdown procedures. She alleged the Defendant owed her a duty of care as a non-client, breached it, and caused her psychiatric injury. The District Court dismissed the proceedings and ordered costs against the Plaintiff.

Key holding: A law firm retained by an institutional client does not owe a third-party complainant a duty of care merely because it investigates that complainant’s concerns; such a relationship falls outside established duty categories and is assessed as a novel duty by salient features.

In my opinion, the relationship between the Plaintiff and the Defendant does not fall within any established categories of relationship that give rise to a duty of care. The Plaintiff was a third party to the professional/client relationship between the Defendant and SCS.

entry.title: Zvicer v Hunter New England Local Health District [2026] NSWSC 1241
entry.content:
Ms Zvicer sued Hunter New England Local Health District alleging that hospital doctors negligently failed to perform a fasciotomy on her left lower leg on 11 November 2020, causing a below-knee amputation. Her children separately claimed psychiatric injury. The Supreme Court dismissed all claims, rejecting liability.

Key holding: A defendant is not liable in negligence for harm that is the materialisation of an inherent risk, being a risk that could not be avoided by reasonable care and skill.

A person is not liable in negligence for harm suffered by another person as a result of the materialisation of an inherent risk.

entry.title: Soar Development Group Pty Ltd v Fung [2026] FCA 1491
entry.content:
Soar sought leave to amend its originating application and statement of claim in a Federal Court commercial proceeding, including professional negligence and knowing assistance claims against EFG and Mr Huang. The first to fourth respondents did not oppose, but EFG and Mr Huang opposed certain amendments on delay and prejudice grounds, saying they materially enlarged the case and loss shortly before a combined hearing.

Key holding: The court may grant leave to amend closed pleadings under rr 8.21 and 16.53 in the exercise of a broad discretion informed by the overarching purpose, and may impose conditions including costs and timetable relief to address delay and prejudice.

An order granting leave may be made subject to conditions: r 1.33. The discretion to grant leave is broad, but must be exercised in a manner consistent with the overarching purpose stated in s 37M of the Federal Court of Australia Act 1976 (Cth) (FCA Act), namely to facilitate the just resolution of disputes according to law and as quickly, inexpensively and efficiently as possible.

entry.title: Mellick v Samarasekera and Ors [2026] NSWSC 1239
entry.content:
This was an application in the Supreme Court of New South Wales for expedition of medical negligence proceedings brought by George Mellick, by his tutor, against two general practitioners and South Western Sydney Local Health District. The plaintiff is 21 years old, has a limited life expectancy and remains at risk of sudden death. The Court granted expedition, fixed an expedited hearing and made case-management directions.

Key holding: In fixing an expedited hearing date that will impose intense preparation burdens, the plaintiff’s health is the primary consideration where the parties agree an early date is required.

I appreciate fixing the matter for hearing on 15 March 2027 will visit an intense period of preparation upon the parties and that some counsel will have to be swapped out due to prior professional commitments, however in all the circumstances the health of the plaintiff needs to be the primary consideration here and the parties have agreed that an early date needs to be accommodated.

entry.title: Youssef & Ors v Dr Sekharipuram Ramamvrthi Govind Krishna [2026] NSWSC 1253
entry.content:
Coleman J approved settlements of claims brought by two minor plaintiffs, Isaiah (16) and Savannah (14), against Dr Krishna for pure mental harm/nervous shock allegedly arising from witnessing their mother’s complications after bariatric surgery. The proceedings were conducted by their father as tutor. Because the plaintiffs are under legal incapacity, the settlements required court approval under s 76(4) of the Civil Procedure Act 2005 (NSW).

Key holding: On an application to approve a settlement for a person under legal incapacity, the court’s protective function requires it to determine whether the settlement is beneficial to that person’s interests.

The Court's function on such an application is essentially protective. The Court ought to review the terms of settlement or compromise to protect the interests of the persons under the legal incapacity

entry.title: Frazer v State of Queensland [2026] QSC 82 (22 April 2026)
entry.content:
Ms Frazer, an experienced teacher, sued the State of Queensland after suffering PTSD following an incident where an aggrieved parent attended the school looking to confront her. The State admitted it owed a non-delegable duty of care to Ms Frazer, but disputed breach. The court found no breach and entered judgment for the defendant.

Key holding: A policy authorising physical force to remove an abusive or threatening person does not require force in every circumstance; reasonableness depends on the unfolding situation.

It seems to me that the authorisation in Chief Executive Guideline No 1 of 2012 to take all reasonable steps including physical force to eject an abusive, threatening or disorderly person does not, could not and should not demand in all circumstances that physical force be used to eject an abusive, threatening or disorderly person.

entry.title: Holzer v Homes Victoria [2026] VCC 472 (17 April 2026)
entry.content:
In Holzer v Homes Victoria [2026] VCC 472, the defendant applied shortly before a jury trial for leave to amend its defence in a negligence proceeding. The proposed amendment sought to plead reasonable inspection, reporting, cleaning and maintenance systems and delegation to contractors GJ & K Cleaning Services and McPeake. The County Court allowed the amendment in the interests of justice, despite an unsatisfactory explanation, with consequential orders to follow.

Key holding: On an application for leave to amend, the ultimate question is what the justice of the case requires.

The ultimate question in determining such an application is what the justice of the case requires.

entry.title: VWA v Homes Victoria [2026] VCC 471 (17 April 2026)
entry.content:
VWA v Homes Victoria [2026] VCC 471 is a County Court ruling on Homes Victoria’s application to amend its defence in a negligence proceeding. The proposed amendment expands the original bare denial to plead reasonable systems for inspection, reporting, cleaning and maintenance, and reliance on cleaning and maintenance contractors. The Court allowed the application, holding that the justice of the case favoured amendment; the proceeding cannot currently proceed pending consequential orders.

Key holding: On an application for leave to amend a defence, the Court must determine what the justice of the case requires by weighing the relevant considerations and should allow the amendment if the interests of justice favour it.

The ultimate question in determining such an application is what the justice of the case requires. Having conducted the balancing exercise required of me, I find that it is in the interests of justice to allow the proposed amendment.

entry.title: Sheather v V & E Bozzi & Co Transport Pty Ltd (Ruling No 1) [2026] VSC 203 (10 April 2026)
entry.content:
Mike Sheather sued V & E Bozzi & Co Transport Pty Ltd for injuries suffered at Texas Downs, NSW, after the defendant had admitted employment and a Victorian workers compensation claim had been accepted. On the eve of trial the defendant sought leave to withdraw that admission and allege employment by Bozzi Produce, or alternatively to issue a third party notice against Bozzi Produce. Gorton J refused withdrawal but allowed the third party notice and vacated the trial date.

Key holding: On a late application to withdraw an admission, the court exercises its discretion by assessing where justice lies, including the extent to which allowing the amendment would cause substantial delay or unfair prejudice to the opposing party.

Particularly in the case of a late amendment such as this, that includes an assessment of whether or the extent to which the amendment if allowed would cause substantial delay or other unfair prejudice to the plaintiff.

entry.title: Gong v AWI Steel Pty Limited [2026] NSWSC 331 (9 April 2026)
entry.content:
Mr Gong, a boilermaker/welder supplied to AWI Steel’s factory via labour-hire arrangements, was injured when a heavy steel plate slipped and fell on his foot. He sued AWI in negligence; AWI denied duty/breach and alleged contributory negligence. The Supreme Court found AWI liable but reduced damages for Mr Gong’s contributory negligence, with AWI bearing the greater responsibility.

Key holding: A principal or occupier that organises, controls and supervises work at its premises owes a duty of reasonable care to independent contractor workers to avoid unnecessary risk of injury.

AWI's duty being to use reasonable care to avoid unnecessary risk of injury to all those who worked together at its factory, including the Ebenezer workers, given the risk of harm to which they were exposed, given the work AWI' had them perform there.

entry.title: Woolnough v Whittlesea City Council & Anor [2026] VSC 190 (7 April 2026)
entry.content:
In Woolnough v Whittlesea City Council & Anor [2026] VSC 190, a young cricketer suffered catastrophic injuries after falling while vaulting a boundary fence at a council reserve during training. The Supreme Court of Victoria held the Council negligent for failing to install a pedestrian gate adjacent to the new nets, but found the Cricket Club not negligent and reduced damages by 20% for contributory negligence.

Key holding: In occupier negligence, a failure to install a modest pedestrian gate can be unreasonable where the occupier knows or ought to know that many users will foreseeably and repeatedly jump a boundary fence at that location, because the aggregate risk of injury—not merely the risk of a single jump—is relevant to the reasonableness calculus.

Further, and although, as noted, for most reasonably fit people, climbing or jumping over a fence on a single occasion carries only a very small risk of injury, the risk of injury is much greater when these single occasions are aggregated, as would be the case if, for example, every member of every football team were to jump or climb over the fence before and after each game and training session over multiple seasons.

Supreme Court of Victoria, 7 Apr 2026, [2026] VSC 190

entry.title: ORION RESOURCES PTY LTD -v- ROBERT CONRY BRAUER AND WILLIAM JAMES HARRIS AS JOINT AND SEVERAL RECEIVERS AND MANAGERS OF AUSMEX RESOURCES PTY LTD ACN 618 778 822 (IN LIQUIDATION) (RECEIVERS AND MANAGERS APPOINTED) AS JOINT AND SEVERAL RECEIVERS AND MANAGERS OF TOMBOLA GOLD LTD ACN 148 860 299 (SUBJECT TO DEED OF COMPANY ARRANGEMENT) (RECEIVERS AND MANAGERS APPOINTED) AS JOINT AND SEVERAL RECEIVERS AND MANAGERS OF AUSMEX MINING PTY LTD ACN 612 797 396 (IN LIQUIDATION) (RECEIVERS AND MANAGERS APPOINTED) [2026] WASC 107 (2 April 2026)
entry.content:
Orion Resources Pty Ltd sued the receivers/managers, liquidators and administrators of the Tombola/AusMex group after the Cloncurry Gold Project asset sale agreement terminated on 14 November 2025. Orion sought leave under the Corporations Act to proceed against and join companies in liquidation, a declaration that termination was invalid, specific performance, an injunction and negligence damages. Hill J refused leave and entered summary judgment for the first to third defendants.

Key holding: A party cannot invalidate automatic termination under a later variation agreement by relying on earlier alleged breaches where the later agreement varied the relevant obligations and termination occurred through that party’s failure to comply with the later payment deadline.

Given each of these matters, even if the plaintiff were able to establish at trial each of the matters in [27(a)] to [27(d)] of the proposed amended statement of claim, this would not mean the termination of the ASA under the express terms of the ERT Agreement was invalid.

entry.title: Julie Rawlins v Coca Cola Europacific Partners Australia Pty Ltd [2026] VCC 341 (30 March 2026)
entry.content:
Julie Rawlins claimed she injured her right thumb on 23 April 2020 while “facing up” two-litre soft drink bottles in her role with Coca-Cola Europacific Partners. A jury found negligence for that incident, but the defendant applied for judgment non obstante veredicto under s 70(2) of the County Court Act 1958 (Vic). The County Court granted the application and entered judgment for the defendant on Question 1.

Key holding: In a claim alleging an employer’s failure to provide a safe system of work, the plaintiff must prove by evidence that a reasonably practicable alternative system was available, should have been used, and would have reduced or avoided the risk of injury.

The plaintiff had also to prove by evidence that a reasonably practicable alternative system of work which would have reduced or avoided the risk of injury was available to the employer and should have been utilised.

entry.title: Agnello v Maliganis Edwards Johnson (No 2) [2026] ACTSC 84 (27 March 2026)
entry.content:
Mr Agnello sued his former solicitors, Maliganis Edwards Johnson, for professional negligence after settling his ACT workers compensation claim for $420,000 in April 2017. He alleged the firm failed to properly advise him about his rights and the risks of commutation before settlement. The Supreme Court found breach in one respect but dismissed the claim because causation was not established.

Key holding: In a professional negligence claim against solicitors, breach alone is insufficient; the client must prove that the solicitor’s failure to advise caused the client’s loss, including that proper advice would have produced a different settlement outcome.

breach established with respect to the risk of commutation with respect to opinion contained within report - causation not established - failure to provide advice did not cause harm - value of the lost opportunity - proceedings dismissed

entry.title: R v Sabra [2026] NSWDC 70 (27 March 2026)
entry.content:
Abbas Sabra was acquitted by a jury of dangerous driving causing death, and the District Court then determined a back-up charge of negligent driving occasioning death under s 117(1)(a) Road Transport Act 2013 (NSW). The Crown alleged he failed to keep a proper lookout, but the judge found the Crown had not proved beyond reasonable doubt that the deceased was still crossing the road rather than moving from the median strip into his path. The accused was found not guilty.

Key holding: The Crown must prove beyond reasonable doubt any inferential finding essential to guilt, and if the inference relied on is not the only reasonably available inference, the charge is not proved.

Accordingly, I am not satisfied that the inference of fact contended for by the Crown is the only reasonably available inference from the primary facts. I am not satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that Mrs Nasr was still in the process of crossing the road, which in accordance with the direction I have given myself, is an essential finding for the Crown's case, and of itself is sufficient to conclude that the Accused is not guilty.

entry.title: Lofts v Lawcover Insurance Pty Limited [2026] NSWDC 68 (20 March 2026)
entry.content:
The plaintiff, the deceased’s only child, sued Lawcover as insurer of the solicitors who prepared his father’s will. The will scheme gave the deceased’s de facto partner a life estate in the Forster Property, with the deceased’s interest then passing to the plaintiff, but the property was held in joint tenancy, so it passed by survivorship outside the estate. The court found the solicitors negligently failed to advise on or implement severance of the joint tenancy and awarded $510,000.

Key holding: A solicitor retained to prepare a will can owe a tortious duty to an intended beneficiary to advise on, and take reasonable steps to implement, severance of a joint tenancy where that is integral to carrying out the testator’s communicated testamentary intention.

The fact of the joint tenancy meant that, unless it was severed before either of Mr Lofts or Ms Miller died, the scheme in cl 3 would fail. A competent solicitor exercising reasonable care in the drafting of the Will would have advised their clients of that fact and, unless that testamentary intention was changed, provided their clients with the means to have the joint tenancy severed.

entry.title: Zioukin v Bellissimo t/as Bellissimo Lawyers and Studio Legale [2026] NSWDC 54 (20 March 2026)
entry.content:
Andre Zioukin sued Frank Bellissimo, his former solicitor, alleging negligence because the earlier police tort proceedings did not include a personal injuries claim and settled by Deed for $15,000 plus costs. The District Court found the no-personal-injury strategy was an advertent, instructed decision driven by costs-capping and commercial viability, and that any hypothetical personal injuries claim would have failed. Judgment was entered for the solicitor.

Key holding: A solicitor is not negligent for omitting a personal injuries claim where the decision to proceed without it was made on the client’s instructions.

I thus find that the defendant was not negligent in advancing a case in the Police Proceedings which did not include a claim for personal injuries, as the decision to proceed in that manner was made on the plaintiff's instructions.

entry.title: McMahon v Balint-Smith [2026] VCC 297 (20 March 2026)
entry.content:
The plaintiff was injured when the defendant’s dog, Georgie, collided with her left knee at McCrae Beach, causing a tibial plateau fracture and later total knee replacement. The County Court found the defendant negligent for failing to manage and control Georgie and entered judgment for the plaintiff. Quantum is not discernible from the supplied extract.

Key holding: A dog owner must exercise reasonable care in managing and controlling the dog to avoid reasonably foreseeable injury, and failing to restrain or recall a fast dog running uncontrolled close to people can be negligent.

What I am required to decide in this case is whether the defendant exercised reasonable care in his management and control of Georgie to ensure that Georgie did not cause the plaintiff a reasonably foreseeable injury. I find that the defendant failed to exercise such reasonable care.
